A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CorePipe and CoreCodeBench, retaining the same underlying repositories and task taxonomy despite a changed title and substantial revision. Both complete 23-page documents, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, were readable.

before.justification: V1 reports original LLM evaluations, human quality inspection and generator-selection experiments, including Tables 3–4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: V2 reports original model evaluations and additional empirical analyses, including prompt robustness, task correlations and the fine-tuning experiment in Appendix K.

M1.justification: The core pipeline retains call-tree extraction, AST masking, generated descriptions with critique and IG filtering, cascaded bug synthesis, and composite-task construction. V2 expands descriptions of these components without establishing a different generation algorithm. Its new fine-tuning experiment validates the benchmark rather than introducing a proposed training method.

E1.justification: The twelve Python repositories and six core task types remain. V2 adds comparative coverage through score-based analysis of eight external algorithmic and engineering benchmarks, including HumanEvalPlus, MultiPL-E and SWE-bench (Section 4.6). This documents analysis of external benchmark results, without establishing that those evaluations were newly run.

E2.justification: V1's sixteen-model main comparison is largely replaced by nine newer models, including GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Pro, Kimi-K2 and DeepSeek-V3.2. V2 Appendix L reports twelve models, retaining Claude-3.7 and Llama-3.1 there. Appendix D also adds a direct GPT-4o bug-generation comparator.

E3.justification: V2 replaces model-specific recommended/default decoding with uniform greedy decoding at temperature 0 and top_p 1.0. It adds an eleven-repository training/one-repository testing protocol and new correlation, consistency and prompt-variation procedures. The stated repository test-file threshold changes from over 30% to over 15%, and the BugFix count changes from 317 to 315.

E4.justification: V2 adds low-IG subset evaluation, a bug-realism case comparison, a 50-sample core-code audit, prompt-rephrasing and context-length robustness analyses, fine-tuning validation, difficulty-scaling curves, and task/external-benchmark correlations and clustering. The generator-sensitivity heatmap already existed in v1; its relocation and stronger discussion are not a new experiment.

E5.justification: V1 largely reports point estimates. V2 introduces systematic 95% confidence intervals, explains their repository-equal computation in Appendix L, and compares prompt variation against uncertainty. It also newly reports over 95% annotator agreement and 50% annotation cross-verification. These additions do not establish increased repeated-run or seed counts.

E6.justification: Leaderboards are extensively replaced, and fine-tuning, robustness and correlation results are added. Retained Claude-3.7's Development AC@1 changes from 63.59 in v1 Table 3 to 52.81 in v2 Table 9; changed inference settings prevent interpreting this as a controlled performance decline. V1's repository-level result tables are removed.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix L.1 adds an explicit repository-independence assumption and a mathematical construction combining repository-level standard errors into normal-approximation confidence intervals. V1 only describes averaging performance across repositories. The underlying AC Rate and IG equations remain equivalent despite terminology changes.

C1.justification: V1 primarily contributes a configurable multi-scenario engineering benchmark and already observes differing model capabilities. V2 makes stronger claims about isolating cognitive dimensions, contamination resilience, preventing saturation, superiority over SWE-bench-Verified's retention rate, and measuring capabilities distinct from existing benchmarks. These substantially expand the claimed scientific contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations about fragmented capability profiles, semantic complexity versus context length, alignment-related resistance to generating bugs, and fine-tuning as evidence of valid supervision. It newly identifies selection bias toward well-tested projects and explicitly limits ranking confidence for the ten-instance Multi-BugFix subset, beyond v1's broader testing and Python limitations.

D1.justification: V2 adds the core-code selection prompt and model, detailed annotation criteria, vLLM inference information, Docker execution specifications, a 120-second timeout, and fine-tuning optimizer, precision, batch-size and sequence-length settings. Dockerfiles and setup scripts are promised upon publication. These substantially expand documentation without establishing that every disclosed setting changed.

R1.justification: V2 expands references to work including LiveCodeBench, FEA-Bench, RepoTransBench and MigrationBench. More substantially, it positions CoreCodeBench against static, supposedly monolithic evaluations and argues for distinct capability coverage using external-benchmark correlations. This goes beyond v1's emphasis on multi-scenario coverage and controllable benchmark construction.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial portions of the methods and discussion are rewritten. Experiments are organized around four research questions, related work moves toward the end, limitations become separate, and appendices are reorganized and expanded. Single-function/multi-function terminology is recast as atomic/composite tasks.

P2.justification: V2 switches to a two-column layout, redraws the pipeline illustration, adds conceptual and analytical figures, and replaces the radar presentation with correlation and consistency displays. Repository-level tables disappear while uncertainty, robustness, fine-tuning and annotation tables appear. Existing generator examples and sensitivity figures are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: New fine-tuning and robustness studies, uncertainty reporting, and execution and annotation details improve validation and reproducibility. The net gain is limited by lost repository-level results and overstated conclusions: Section 4.2 claims five improved fine-tuning metrics, whereas Table 8 shows four improvements, one unchanged metric and one decline. The prominent 78.55% versus 31.7% quality comparison also contrasts differently defined qualification and retention measures.
